Real-Time Whole-Body Control of Legged R.narr: Running a legged robot requires controlling dozens of joints at kHz rates to keep the robot upright and move it forward. Classical MPC solves a quadratic program at each timestep, but solving it accurately takes too long. This paper applies GPU-parallel sampling — instead of solving one optimization exactly, sample thousands of random action sequences on the GPU, weight them by cost, and take the mean — making real-time whole-body control on expensive hardware unnecessary.
Real-Time Whole-Body Control of Legged R.how:
The Problem: A legged robot's dynamics are nonlinear and high-dimensional; solving the full nonlinear MPC at kHz is intractable on embedded CPUs.

The Mechanism: Model-Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) samples K=1000+ random control trajectories over a horizon of N steps, evaluates each under the learned dynamics model, and computes a cost-weighted mean: u* = (1/Z) ∑ w(τ_k) τ_k, where w(τ) = exp(−(1/λ) Cost(τ)). All K rollouts run in parallel on a GPU; the mean is computed in a few milliseconds.

Why It Works: GPU parallelism turns gradient-free optimization into a sampling problem. No Jacobian computation, no line search, no interior-point algorithm — just parallel forward rollouts and a weighted average. This trades accuracy for speed: MPPI is noisier than a QP solver but runs fast enough to close the loop at control rates.

Flying Quadrotors in Tight Formations Us.narr: When multiple quadrotors fly in formation, each drone's thrust affects its neighbors via aerodynamic downwash. A pure first-principles model cannot capture this coupling. This paper augments the MPC's prediction model with a neural network that learns inter-vehicle aerodynamic effects from data, so the controller anticipates how nearby drones will push it and pre-compensates.
Flying Quadrotors in Tight Formations Us.how:
The Problem: Aerodynamic coupling between drones is complex and model-mismatch causes formation spacing to grow beyond acceptable bounds.

The Mechanism: Train a neural network f_NN(s_i, s_neighbors) → Δa_coupling on logged flight data to predict how each neighbor's thrust adds extra acceleration to the focal drone. Modify the MPC's prediction model to include this term: a_aug = a_phys(s,u) + f_NN(s, neighbor_states). The MPC solver sees the augmented model and plans trajectories that account for coupling.

Why It Works: The neural network learns the nonlinear aerodynamic interactions that first-principles models miss. By incorporating the learned coupling into the lookahead model, the controller can predict future collisions earlier and steer away before they happen, reducing spacing variance in tight formation from 0.8 m to 0.09 m.

Dynamic Tube MPC: Learning Tube Dynamics.narr: A physics model is never perfect, but conservative MPC that assumes worst-case error wastes performance by shrinking constraints. This paper learns the actual envelope of reachable states under model error using GPU simulation, then uses that learned tube to give real safety guarantees without over-conservatism.
Dynamic Tube MPC: Learning Tube Dynamics.how:
The mechanism: Sample thousands of trajectories in parallel on a GPU, each with slightly different model parameters (within the uncertainty set). Track the reachable set at each timestep — the union of all sampled states. This learned tube is tighter than the worst-case tube because it exploits structure in how errors actually occur, not just bounds.

At runtime, MPC solves with the learned tube constraints. Since the tube was computed offline, the online solve cost is unchanged. The robot gets safety guarantees (states stay in the computed tube) with less conservative motion.

Parallel-Constraint Model Predictive Con.narr: As a robot navigates through dense obstacle fields, the number of collision-avoidance constraints grows quadratically with the number of obstacles and horizon length, slowing the MPC solver. This paper parallelizes constraint evaluation across the horizon on multiple CPU cores or a GPU, so the QP solver can handle dozens of obstacles in real time.
Parallel-Constraint Model Predictive Con.how:
The Problem: For a horizon N and M obstacles, there are O(N·M) collision constraints; evaluating and passing them to the QP solver dominates the solve time when M is large.

The Mechanism: Instead of building the full constraint matrix sequentially, divide the horizon into chunks and evaluate constraints for each chunk in parallel. Each thread checks collision for its timestep range against all obstacles. Assemble the sparse constraint matrix from the parallel outputs and pass to the QP solver. Total wall time is horizon-length / num_cores instead of sequential.

Why It Works: Constraint evaluation is embarrassingly parallel — each timestep's constraints depend only on that timestep's state, not on others. By parallelizing this naturally parallel loop, the MPC can afford many more constraints and thus handle denser obstacle fields without missing control deadlines.

High Accuracy Aerial Maneuvers on Legged.narr: Long-horizon trajectory optimization with standard numerical integration drifts energy over many steps — a planned backflip that is energy-exact in the continuous system loses 0.8% total mechanical energy by step 150, causing the plan to fail on hardware. Variational integrators discretize Hamilton's principle so the discrete system exactly conserves energy, making plans trustworthy.
High Accuracy Aerial Maneuvers on Legged.how:
The mechanism: Instead of discretizing the dynamics equations (Euler, RK4), discretize the action functional S = ∫ L dt via a summation. Use a Legendre transform to get discrete equations that are symplectic (a structure-preserving property). The result: the discrete system has a conserved energy that matches the continuous system to machine precision.

Trajectory optimization uses this symplectic discretization, so the optimizer plans a trajectory whose energy is conserved. When that trajectory is executed on hardware (which also conserves energy), the plan matches reality. Backflip success rate jumps from 51% to 87%.

Endpoint-Explicit Differential Dynamic P.narr: Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) is a fast trajectory optimizer, but it typically enforces endpoint constraints (e.g., end position = goal) as a soft penalty, which can lead to slow convergence or infeasible solutions. This paper modifies DDP to enforce endpoint constraints exactly at every iteration, improving convergence speed and guaranteeing feasibility.
Endpoint-Explicit Differential Dynamic P.how:
The Problem: A soft terminal cost may conflict with the backward-pass quadratic approximation, causing the algorithm to oscillate near the constraint rather than converge cleanly.

The Mechanism: (1) In the backward pass, after computing the cost-to-go value function V_k(x_k), check if the terminal constraint is satisfied. (2) If not, modify the terminal condition to enforce the constraint exactly: replace the soft terminal cost with a hard constraint x_N = x_goal, then back-substitute into the Bellman equation. (3) This gives a quadratic cost-to-go at t=N-1 that is consistent with the constraint. (4) Forward pass then finds gains that satisfy the constraint exactly at convergence.

Why It Works: Closing the loop exactly prevents the algorithm from circling around the constraint boundary. The optimizer converges faster and the final trajectory is guaranteed to reach the endpoint, not just approach it asymptotically.

Near Time-Optimal Hybrid Motion Planning.narr: A timber crane has a cable that can be either in tension (taut) or slack. Switching between these modes creates hybrid dynamics — the system transitions discontinuously between regimes. DDP is designed for smooth dynamics, so applying it directly fails. This paper extends DDP to handle mode switches by treating the discrete mode as an additional variable to optimize.
Near Time-Optimal Hybrid Motion Planning.how:
The Problem: Hybrid systems have discrete modes (cable taut/slack) with different continuous dynamics; the solution must specify both the continuous trajectory and the discrete mode schedule.

The Mechanism: (1) Augment the state to include mode indicators: x_aug = (position, velocity, mode ∈ {taut, slack}). (2) Modify the forward dynamics to check at each step: if the cable is slack and the constraint becomes active, switch to taut. (3) Modify the backward pass to compute value functions for each mode separately, then take a min-over-modes step: V_k(x) = min(V_k^{taut}(x), V_k^{slack}(x)). (4) This gives discontinuous value functions at mode boundaries, which DDP can still optimize through via mode-transition detection.

Why It Works: By treating mode transitions as discrete decisions subject to continuous dynamics, the algorithm can find trajectories that exploit mode switching to reduce time. The trajectory automatically discovers when to let the cable go slack (reducing drag) and when to engage it (changing direction) to minimize travel time.

Learning Time-Optimal Online Replanning.narr: Centralized MPC for multi-quadrotor contouring (tracing a path shape while maintaining formation) scales poorly. Each quadrotor runs its own MPC, but must predict neighbors' future positions to avoid collision. This paper has each quadrotor learn a local replanning policy that adapts its contouring path to neighbors' predicted trajectories.
Learning Time-Optimal Online Replanning.how:
The mechanism: Each quadrotor solves a small local MPC (12-state) that optimizes its path subject to soft constraints for neighbor predictions. The predicted trajectories come via wireless broadcast — each neighbor sends its 20-step predicted trajectory. The local MPC includes these as moving obstacle constraints.

A policy network (trained offline) learns to adjust the time-optimal parametrization of the contour based on the current obstacle set. This replaces manual gain tuning with learned replanning, and runs at 50 Hz on each drone's onboard computer.

Passivity Filters for Bilateral Teleoper.narr: In teleoperated robotics, a human operator controls a remote robot via a haptic device. If the network has delay, the feedback loop can become unstable — energy keeps flowing from the operator's end to the robot, causing oscillations. This paper ensures stability by embedding a passivity filter that dissipates excess energy, even when the operator changes the compliance in the middle of a task.
Passivity Filters for Bilateral Teleoper.how:
The Problem: Variable impedance (stiffness) can introduce more energy into the loop, breaking passivity assumptions used to prove stability.

The Mechanism: (1) Model the teleoperator as two ports: operator-side (position/force in, position/force out) and robot-side (likewise). (2) Compute the instantaneous power flowing into each port: P_op = F_op · v_op, P_robot = F_robot · v_robot. (3) Insert a dissipative element that removes power when total energy is positive: E_stored += (P_op + P_robot) dt; if E_stored > E_threshold, extract power by adding damping to both sides. (4) Adjust damping in real-time as impedance changes.

Why It Works: Passivity is a fundamental guarantee in nonlinear control: if energy never leaves the system, it cannot oscillate unboundedly. The filter preserves passivity despite variable impedance by actively dissipating energy when too much builds up, keeping the system stable under network delay.

Bipedal Walking with Continuously Compli.narr: A rigid-leg biped bounces unpredictably on uneven ground because each impact is a sudden shock. Real legs have springs (tendons) that absorb impacts smoothly. This paper models the legs as spring-damper systems with the spring in series with the motor, so the motor drives the spring but the spring deflects at contact, absorbing impact energy passively.
Bipedal Walking with Continuously Compli.how:
The Problem: Rigid legs transmit impact shock directly to the body, requiring the controller to react instantly; compliant legs absorb some impact before the body feels it.

The Mechanism: (1) Replace rigid joint dynamics with: motor position q_m, link position q_l, spring torque τ_s = k(q_m − q_l). (2) Link dynamics: I_link · q_l_ddot = τ_s − F_contact. Motor command u drives q_m. (3) When the foot contacts ground at high speed, F_contact is large, but the spring can deflect, so q_l changes slowly initially. (4) The spring-leg acts as a mechanical impedance that absorbs energy without requiring active control.

Why It Works: Passive spring compliance decouples impact from body acceleration, reducing the peak accelerations that the robot's sensors and actuators must handle. The spring naturally distributes force over time instead of applying a delta-function impulse, stabilizing the gait on rough terrain without active feedback.

Watch Less, Feel More: Sim-to-Real RL fo.narr: A robot learning to manipulate objects from simulation often fails on real objects because the contact is too stiff — the sim doesn't match reality. This paper combines two ideas: learn impedance gains in simulation to make the sim contact feel realistic, and use impedance to absorb contact mismatches so the learned policy transfers without modification.
Watch Less, Feel More: Sim-to-Real RL fo.how:
The Problem: Sim-to-real gap for manipulation is large; the learned controller is brittle to contact surprises because it relies on stiff position control.

The Mechanism: (1) Train the RL policy in simulation with randomized object parameters and dynamics. (2) During training, the controller outputs not just desired joint positions but also desired stiffness K_desired. (3) Let the RL optimizer choose K_desired to maximize task success. (4) Implement the policy on real hardware using impedance control: F = K_desired · (q_desired − q_actual) + B · (qd_desired − qd_actual). (5) The learned impedance profile absorbs contact mismatches; high stiffness during free motion, low stiffness during contact.

Why It Works: Impedance is a low-level compliance that the RL algorithm learns as part of the policy. When the real robot contacts something unexpected, the low impedance yields smoothly instead of fighting, so the overall policy is reliable to contact errors that would break a position-stiff controller.

Optimal Framework for Constrained Admitt.narr: A robot following a path while also maintaining compliance (admittance to external forces) faces a conflict: compliance means yielding to forces, but path-following means ignoring them. This paper optimizes the admittance gains such that the robot follows the path while being as compliant as possible without straying.
Optimal Framework for Constrained Admitt.how:
The Problem: High admittance makes the robot yield to disturbances and leave the path; high stiffness keeps the path but cannot absorb contact.

The Mechanism: (1) Define the control law: F = K(x_desired − x_actual) + B(v_desired − v_actual), where x_desired is on the path. (2) Admittance is 1/K; lower K = higher admittance. (3) Optimize a cost: min_K ∫ (||e_path(t)||² + λ·||contact_force(t)||²) dt, where the first term penalizes path-following error and the second encourages low contact forces (thus high admittance). (4) Solve as a QP: find K that minimizes the weighted sum subject to constraints e_path < ε_max (hard path constraint).

Why It Works: By casting admittance tuning as an optimization, the controller finds the sweet spot: just stiff enough to follow the path, just compliant enough to absorb contact forces without fighting them. The result is both path-accurate and contact-safe.

Reduced-Order Model Guided Contact-Impli.narr: Humanoid walking is complex — the robot must balance on two feet while moving dozens of joints. A full-body MPC takes too long to solve. This paper uses a simple reduced-order model (like an inverted pendulum) to guide a full-body trajectory, then solves a contact-implicit QP to track the reference while discovering which feet to use for contact.
Reduced-Order Model Guided Contact-Impli.how:
The Problem: Full-body MPC for humanoid is too slow; contact mode enumeration (which feet touch) is combinatorial.

The Mechanism: (1) Use a reduced-order model (LIP + torso) to quickly plan a reference CoM trajectory over a long horizon. (2) At each MPC solve, take a local window (5-10 steps ahead) and optimize the full-body QP: min_τ ||J_CoM·τ − a_ref|| + ||J_hand·τ − a_hand|| + ... subject to τ_limits, contact wrench in friction cone. (3) Formulate contact as a soft penalty, not a hard mode switch: instead of 2^n mode-branches, the QP finds continuous contact forces that sum to zero if the foot lifts and nonzero if it touches. (4) This automatically selects contact implicitly.

Why It Works: The reduced model provides a fast long-horizon plan; the full-body QP refines it locally and auto-selects contact. Contact is discovered by the optimization, not enumerated, so complex gaits with multiple simultaneous contacts are found without exploring exponentially many mode combinations.

A Control Barrier Function for Safe Navi.narr: A robot navigating an unknown environment builds an occupancy map as it moves. The map is uncertain — it updates as new measurements arrive. A control barrier function (CBF) is a safety constraint that guarantees the robot never enters occupied space, even if the map suddenly changes. This paper embeds a CBF in the control QP with an online-updating occupancy map.
A Control Barrier Function for Safe Navi.how:
The Problem: A QP can enforce occupancy constraints, but if the map updates mid-trajectory, the robot might be inside an obstacle before the next solve.

The Mechanism: (1) Define a barrier function h(x) = (signed distance from robot to nearest obstacle). (2) A CBF constraint is: dh/dt ≥ −γ·h, which ensures h remains positive (robot outside obstacles). (3) Rewrite in terms of control: J·u ≥ −γ·h − ∂h/∂x·f_nominal, where J is the Jacobian of h w.r.t. control. (4) Add this as a linear inequality constraint in the QP: find u minimizing tracking error subject to CBF constraint + dynamics limits. (5) Solve at kHz, updating h from the Gaussian splatting map at each timestep.

Why It Works: The CBF constraint is a sufficient condition for safety: if it holds, h stays positive forever. By enforcing it in the real-time QP with updated map data, the controller adapts instantly to newly discovered obstacles without abandoning the current motion.

On the Synthesis of Reactive Collision-F.narr: A humanoid must avoid self-collision while moving. Detecting and explicitly listing all potential collisions is expensive. This paper encodes collision-free motion as a complementarity constraint inside the QP — for each pair of links, either they are far apart or they are in contact with zero force, but not both.
On the Synthesis of Reactive Collision-F.how:
The Problem: Enumerating which pairs collide is combinatorial; each pair needs an inequality constraint or it can collide.

The Mechanism: (1) For each link pair (i, j), define distance d_ij(q) and normal force f_n_ij (compression along the surface normal). (2) Complementarity: d_ij·f_n_ij = 0, meaning either d_ij > 0 (no contact) or f_n_ij = 0 (contact but no force). (3) Smooth the complementarity: d_ij·f_n_ij ≤ ε for small ε. (4) Add to the QP: find torques τ and contact forces {f_n_ij} that minimize task cost subject to complementarity constraints + friction cone limits + dynamics. (5) A good solver handles the quasi-smooth complementarity by iterating until it converges.

Why It Works: Complementarity removes the need to decide in advance which pairs collide. The optimizer explores configurations, and the complementarity constraint automatically enforces that if two links get close, their contact force must drop to keep the constraint satisfied. This weeds out configurations where links would collide with nonzero force.

BODex: Scalable and Efficient Robotic De.narr: A dexterous hand can grasp in many ways. Choosing which fingers to use and how hard to squeeze is a complex problem. This paper decomposes grasp synthesis into two levels: an outer loop chooses the approach direction and contact points, and an inner loop solves a QP for the grip forces that satisfy friction and stability constraints.
BODex: Scalable and Efficient Robotic De.how:
The Problem: Grasp planning is continuous (approach direction, contact location) plus discrete (which fingers, which surfaces); full optimization is intractable.

The Mechanism: (1) Outer loop: sample or optimize approach direction θ and candidate contact point locations on the object. (2) For each candidate, solve inner-loop QP: given contact points fixed, find finger forces f_i such that (a) they create a wrench that resists gravity and disturbances (force/torque balance), (b) each force is within the friction cone, (c) minimize finger effort ||f||². (3) Score each candidate: outer loop objective = (inner QP cost) + penalty for infeasibility. (4) Iterate outer loop by gradient descent or sampling; each iteration solves ~10-100 inner QPs.

Why It Works: Bilevel separation turns a hard hybrid optimization into a sequence of convex QPs (inner loop) wrapped in a smooth search (outer loop). The inner QP is fast enough that the outer loop can afford many iterations, exploring the space of approaches efficiently without solving the full joint problem.

Koopman Operator Based Linear Model Pred.narr: A quadruped's stance-phase dynamics are highly nonlinear — the ground reaction forces depend on which feet are in contact in a complex way. MPC on the nonlinear model is slow. This paper lifts the state to a higher-dimensional space where the dynamics become approximately linear using the Koopman operator, so MPC becomes a fast linear QP.
Koopman Operator Based Linear Model Pred.how:
The Problem: Nonlinear MPC for stance dynamics requires a nonlinear solver; linearization around a trajectory loses accuracy.

The Mechanism: (1) The Koopman operator K lifts observable functions: if z = K(x) where x is the original state and z is lifted, then z evolves linearly: z_{k+1} = A·z_k + B·u_k. (2) Choose z to include the original 12 state dims plus basis functions: z = [x; x_1²; x_1·x_2; ...] — up to 64 dims. (3) Fit A, B matrices from data: collect trajectories of the quadruped, measure x_k and u_k, fit z_{k+1} = A·z_k + B·u_k in a least-squares sense. (4) MPC in lifted space: min_u ∑_k ||z_k − z_ref||² s.t. z_{k+1} = A·z_k + B·u_k, u ∈ U. (5) Project solution back to original space: x = K^{−1}(z).

Why It Works: The Koopman lifting trades state dimension for linearity. The lifted-space MPC is convex (linear) and solves in <1 ms. Small lifting error is acceptable because the feedback loop corrects it at the next solve; the nonlinear effects are re-linearized continuously.

Optimal Torque Distribution via Dynamic.narr: The friction coefficient determines the maximum horizontal force the foot can exert without slipping — it is the key parameter in the QP's friction cone constraint. On slippery terrain this changes rapidly, but assuming worst-case friction all the time makes the robot overly cautious. This paper estimates friction online from foot slip and updates the QP constraint dynamically.
Optimal Torque Distribution via Dynamic.how:
The mechanism: Estimate friction coefficient μ from the history of measured foot slip: track the discrepancy between commanded force and actual foot acceleration, then fit a least-squares estimate of μ. Update the estimate every 100 ms (aligned with the gait cycle). Feed the estimate into the friction cone constraint in the next QP solve.

The adaptation rate is tuned to the gait frequency so the estimate converges before it becomes stale. On wet grass (μ = 0.3) the estimate converges within 0.5 s; the QP then relaxes horizontal force bounds automatically.

Beyond Robustness: Learning Unknown Dyna.narr: A quadruped's gait works well for its nominal weight but fails when loaded — the legs are too weak or the timing is wrong. Instead of hand-tuning gains for every possible load, this paper learns a meta-learning model that adapts gait parameters online in a handful of steps, without slowing the control rate.
Beyond Robustness: Learning Unknown Dyna.how:
The Problem: Load changes the dynamics; fixed gait gains are suboptimal or unsafe; re-tuning is slow.

The Mechanism: (1) Collect data with the robot at different known masses; train a meta-learning model (e.g., MAML) to output gait parameters (leg stiffness, duty cycle, height) as a function of recent history. (2) The model learns: history of gait metrics (CoP error, slip rate, impact) → parameters. (3) At test time with unknown load: (a) run a few steps with nominal gait, (b) measure the resulting gait metrics, (c) feed them to the meta-model to get adapted parameters, (d) apply parameters at the next gait cycle. (5) The model generalization means new loads are handled in 1-2 steps.

Why It Works: Meta-learning pre-computes the mapping from feedback signals to good parameters. At runtime, the lookup is a single neural network forward pass, which takes microseconds. The gait self-adapts to unknown loads in real time, balancing performance and safety without hand-tuning.

Shape-Adaptive Planning and Control for.narr: A quadrotor whose frame can actively deform changes its center of mass, inertia, and aerodynamic profile mid-flight. A fixed-model MPC cannot anticipate this change. This paper presents online model adaptation inside the control loop: the deformable geometry is measured or commanded, the inertia and aerodynamic model are updated, and the MPC re-solves with the new model at each timestep, allowing aggressive maneuvers that exploit the added shape flexibility.
Shape-Adaptive Planning and Control for.how:
The mechanism operates on the commanded deformation parameters (extension/contraction of flexible links) and the resulting vehicle geometry and inertia. At each 50 Hz control tick, the algorithm updates the 3D pose and moment-of-inertia tensor based on the current link configuration, then solves a nonlinear MPC that predicts how the deformed quadrotor will behave over the next 15 steps under its current and future inertia.
The critical step is online Jacobian recomputation: the effect of control inputs on body rates (angular acceleration) is now inertia-dependent, so the linearized models used in the MPC must be recomputed every cycle from the fresh inertia estimate. Why this works: by treating deformation as a known (measurable or commanded) input rather than an unknown disturbance, the MPC can plan aggressive lean angles and rotations that account for the changing moment arm, enabling acrobatic maneuvers (like rapid spinning during folds) that would violate stability bounds for a rigid frame.

Multirotor Target Tracking through Polic.narr: A quadrotor tracking a moving target using camera feedback must drive the target to a desired image location. The standard approach — compute the target's pose, plan a trajectory, execute — suffers from singularities when the target is fronto-parallel to the camera or at the image boundary. This paper frames visual servoing as policy iteration in image space, learning a direct mapping from image-space error to motor commands without computing 3D pose, sidestepping singularities entirely.
Multirotor Target Tracking through Polic.how:
The mechanism operates on the image coordinates of the target (u, v in pixels) rather than on 3D pose. At each frame (30 Hz), the vision loop computes the target center and its distance from a desired setpoint (e.g., image center). Policy iteration alternates between policy evaluation — predicting how motor commands affect image error — and policy improvement — updating the motor command policy to reduce image error over multiple past frames.
The key step is direct image-space feedback: instead of inverting the camera model to get 3D pose, the controller learns empirically that a leftward target needs rightward tilt, closer targets need upward acceleration, and so on. Why this works: the learned policy implicitly encodes the camera geometry and is reliable to unknown target depth, lighting changes, and camera calibration errors. The singularity problem vanishes because the feedback operates in image coordinates where 'error' is always well-defined, never degenerate, and the controller can learn non-local behaviors that pure geometric inversion cannot capture.

NDOB-Based Control of a UAV with Delta-A.narr: A UAV carrying a robotic arm (delta-parallel manipulator) experiences disturbances from the arm's own motion — when the arm accelerates, the inertial reaction affects the UAV's rotational dynamics. Naive decoupling of aerial and arm control leads to coupling instability. This paper uses nonlinear disturbance observers to estimate and cancel the arm's dynamic effect on the UAV's attitude, keeping the two loops independent and stable without a full-coupled dynamics model.
NDOB-Based Control of a UAV with Delta-A.how:
The mechanism operates on the UAV body rate errors (measured gyro rates vs desired rates) and the arm joint accelerations (inferred from joint command signals). A nonlinear disturbance observer (NDOB) maintains a running estimate of the total rotational disturbance τ_dist = τ_arm_reaction + τ_wind + τ_sensor_bias. At each 1 kHz attitude control tick, the NDOB updates its estimate using the observed rate error via a high-gain feedback loop: d/dt τ̂_dist = K * (ω_meas - ω_desired).
The key step is feedforward cancellation: the estimated disturbance is subtracted from the desired control torque before being sent to the motors, so the effective command seen by the flight controller is the true disturbance-free command. Why this works: the NDOB requires no model of arm inertia or kinematics — it estimates the net effect from body-rate measurements alone. The cancellation is exact when the arm dynamics are captured by the disturbance estimate, which is true for smooth arm motions; the observer converges in a few milliseconds, faster than the arm's bandwidth, so it stays ahead of disturbance changes.

Optimal Trajectory Planning in a Vertica.narr: A snake robot on ridged terrain must coordinate which of its 5 body segments touch the ground in each frame. Explicit contact planning enumerates all 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 modes; implicit methods remove this combinatorial explosion by treating contact as a continuous decision variable. This paper solves a contact-implicit trajectory optimization where the optimizer automatically selects which segments grip at each instant, discovering efficient slithering patterns without mode enumeration.
Optimal Trajectory Planning in a Vertica.how:
The mechanism operates on all 5 segment positions and velocities and a smooth relaxation of the contact constraint. Instead of binary decisions (touching or not), each segment's contact force is allowed to vary continuously. A complementarity-like constraint is smoothed: g(x) * (f · n) ≈ ε, where g is the penetration depth, f is the contact force, and ε is small (0.01). The nonlinear optimizer solves a trajectory that minimizes locomotion time subject to this smooth constraint and friction-cone limits.
The key step is constraint relaxation and tightening: as the solver iterates, it drives ε→0, forcing the solution to snap to contact configurations where either the foot is on the ground (g=0) or the contact force is zero (f=0), but never both partially true. Why this works: the smooth relaxation avoids the combinatorial search over mode trees. The solver naturally selects 3–4 contacts per cycle based on the physics (which segments can reach the ground given the body shape and terrain), producing gait patterns that are stable and efficient, often more creative than hand-designed contact schedules.

Vegetable Peeling: A Case Study in Const.narr: Peeling a vegetable with a dexterous hand requires a sequence of finger contacts on the blade and the vegetable surface, each contact applying forces within friction and grasp-stability limits. The number of possible contact permutations (many fingers, many object locations) is intractable to enumerate. Contact-implicit trajectory optimization discovers the contact strategy by embedding friction and grasp constraints inside a differentiable solver, allowing the optimizer to find blade trajectories that achieve consistent peeling strokes.
Vegetable Peeling: A Case Study in Const.how:
The mechanism operates on blade position and orientation, finger positions (wrist configuration), and contact forces at each potential contact point. The optimization minimizes peeling time subject to: (1) blade must stay in contact with the vegetable surface (smooth penetration penalty), (2) contact forces must lie in friction cones at each finger-vegetable contact and hand-blade contact, (3) no self-collision of fingers, (4) blade motion must follow the surface contour.
The key step is simultaneous contact discovery and force control: the solver jointly optimizes blade trajectory and the contact forces needed to stabilize and guide that trajectory. Contacts that are physically unnecessary for the stroke (too high a cost relative to the motion they enable) naturally drop to zero force. Contacts that are necessary emerge automatically where the physics demands them. Why this works: dexterous manipulation involves so many contact permutations that no engineer can design them all. By making contact forces a continuous optimization variable, the solver explores the space of feasible grasps and strokes, finding ones that balance stability, friction limits, and task goals in a single solve.

A Smooth Analytical Formulation of Colli.narr: Classical rigid-body simulation handles contact with discrete mode-switching logic (is the foot on the ground or not?) and non-smooth complementarity (either a force or zero penetration, but never both). This makes trajectory optimization non-differentiable. This paper provides a smooth analytical model of contact where penetration, forces, and friction all vary continuously, admitting gradients everywhere and enabling end-to-end differentiation through physics.
A Smooth Analytical Formulation of Colli.how:
The mechanism operates on configuration space (joint positions and velocities) and a smooth penetration-penalty model for each potential contact. Instead of the classical hard constraint (penetration = 0) and the Coulomb friction cone (discrete condition), this formulation uses a soft penalty: F_contact = K_stiff * max(0, -h)<sup>2</sup> + B * ḣ, where h is the signed distance (negative = penetrated). The contact force is thus a smooth function of state, with well-defined derivatives everywhere.
The key step is differentiable forward simulation: a trajectory optimizer or policy-learning algorithm can differentiate through the forward dynamics and the contact model to compute ∂x_next/∂u, ∂x_next/∂params, and so on. A gradient-based optimization or neural-network learning loop can then pull contact-implicit trajectories by observing how changes in motion affect contact penetration and force balance. Why this works: smooth formulations sacrifice some physical precision (Coulomb friction is approximated, not exact), but gain the ability to compute gradients. For planning and learning, gradients are far more valuable than perfect friction modeling, because they let the optimizer explore large motion spaces efficiently without resorting to random sampling or mode enumeration.

Autotuning Bipedal Locomotion MPC with G.narr: Legged locomotion MPC models ground reaction forces as optimization variables, but their magnitude depends on unknown ground properties that change between simulation and hardware. This paper trains a neural network to predict ground reaction forces from state, then uses those predictions to auto-tune MPC gains without manual parameter tuning.
Autotuning Bipedal Locomotion MPC with G.how:
The mechanism: GRFM-Net (Ground Reaction Force Model) is a small neural network trained on simulation to map state (positions, velocities, contacts) to predicted foot forces. During MPC, instead of assuming nominal force magnitudes, the network predicts what forces will actually occur, and the QP uses those predictions.

On hardware, the network generalizes to the real ground properties because forces are a physical quantity that transfer across simulation-to-reality if the network has seen enough diversity in training. This replaces manual tuning of force bounds with learned adaptive tuning.

Efficient Online Learning of Contact For.narr: Inserting a connector into a tight socket requires knowing how contact forces vary with insertion depth and angle — parameters that are different for every connector type and socket. Rather than pre-training a universal model, this paper uses online Gaussian process regression during the first few insertions, then lets MPC use the learned model immediately.
Efficient Online Learning of Contact For.how:
The mechanism: A Gaussian process maintains a distribution over the contact force function. As the robot inserts the connector, it observes the actual forces via tactile sensors. Each observation updates the GP posterior, tightening the uncertainty. After just 3–5 insertions, the posterior is sharp enough that MPC can plan tight insertion trajectories.

The key is that learning happens online during the task itself, not in a separate training phase. By the time the operator needs reliable insertion, the model has adapted to this specific connector-socket pair.

DroneDiffusion: Robust Quadrotor Dynamic.narr: Computing a tube that is reliable to non-Gaussian disturbances (e.g., sudden wind gusts) is difficult with classical worst-case methods. This paper uses a diffusion model to learn the actual distribution of aerodynamic disturbances from flight data, then uses that learned distribution to compute a tighter reliable tube.
DroneDiffusion: Robust Quadrotor Dynamic.how:
The mechanism: Train a diffusion model on real flight disturbances. At runtime, the diffusion model generates samples from the learned disturbance distribution. For each disturbance realization, propagate the MPC trajectory forward; the union of all propagated states forms the learned tube. This tube is tighter than worst-case because it only covers plausible disturbances, not every possible disturbance in an interval.

Tube MPC then uses this learned tube as its constraint set. The robot is reliable to the learned distribution, not the worst case, so it can move faster while remaining safe.

Robust Model Predictive Control for Quad.narr: Nominal MPC assumes the model is correct, but quadrupeds encounter mud, slopes, and obstacles that change the dynamics. Tube MPC wraps the nominal solution in a safety envelope computed for the worst-case uncertainty set, but this paper goes further: the tube size adapts online based on how much disturbance is actually measured, reducing over-conservatism.
Robust Model Predictive Control for Quad.how:
The mechanism: Tube MPC precomputes a tightened constraint set such that the nominal solution remains feasible for all uncertainties in a set. But if the actual disturbance is smaller than the worst case, the tube can relax. The algorithm estimates the disturbance magnitude from the state history (e.g., slip detection), then shrinks the tube.

The result: in easy terrain (low disturbance), the tube is loose and the robot moves fast. On slippery terrain, the tube tightens but only as much as needed. This trades off conservatism against adaptability automatically.

Self-Supervised Meta-Learning for All-La.narr: A neural network can learn an adaptive control policy from data, but neural policies lack stability certificates — there is no guarantee the closed-loop system stays bounded. This paper meta-learns a controller whose weights adapt to the observed system, yet embeds a Lyapunov function into the learning objective so stability is guaranteed by construction.
Self-Supervised Meta-Learning for All-La.how:
The mechanism: Meta-learning trains a hypernetwork that maps observed system state to controller weights. The key innovation: the loss includes a Lyapunov penalty — the training objective penalizes any adaptive weight update that would violate V̇ ≤ −αV for a learned quadratic form V. This constraint is enforced during meta-training, not just checked afterward.

The result: the meta-learned adapter is provably stable for any system in a learned region of uncertainty. It adapts faster than fixed-gain controllers because it conditions on the observed dynamics, yet retains the formal guarantees of classical control.

Second-Order Stein Variational Dynamic O.narr: Trajectory optimization via gradient descent gets stuck in local minima. Random restarts help but are expensive. This paper uses particle-based exploration where a swarm of trajectories evolve together, sharing information via a kernel-weighted gradient. Particles repel each other, preventing the whole swarm from collapsing into the same minimum.
Second-Order Stein Variational Dynamic O.how:
The mechanism: Maintain K particles (candidate trajectories), each with its own cost gradient. At each iteration, each particle's update includes two terms: (1) its own gradient (pulling it toward its local minimum) and (2) a repulsion term proportional to the Stein discrepancy between particles (pushing it away from others). This is second-order Stein VDO.

Particles near good minima stay there; particles elsewhere are repelled into different valleys. The algorithm finds higher-quality minima because particles explore in parallel rather than restarting from scratch. For dense environments (crowd navigation), 256 particles find global minima in 12 iterations vs 40 for single-particle gradient descent.

CrowdSurfer: Sampling Optimization Augme.narr: In dense crowds, the space of feasible trajectories is complex and multimodal — the robot could go left, right, or wait, depending on pedestrian motion. SVDO works well but needs good trajectory proposals to start. This paper uses a vector-quantized VAE to generate diverse trajectory proposals by sampling from a learned discrete latent space.
CrowdSurfer: Sampling Optimization Augme.how:
The mechanism: Train a vector-quantized VAE on real crowd navigation trajectories. The latent space is discrete (a codebook of trajectory primitives), so sampling from it gives diverse, realistic proposals. Use these proposals to initialize the particle swarm in SVDO; each particle starts at a different proposal rather than random restarts.

The quantized latent space ensures proposals are well-separated (no two particles start doing nearly the same thing). SVDO then refines them in parallel. This hybrid approach combines learned diversity with optimization refinement, escaping local minima more reliably than pure learning or pure optimization.

CC-STAR: Contact State Transition Estima.narr: During peg insertion, the robot must know when the peg has entered the hole, changed angle, or engaged the chamfer. These contact state transitions are invisible to proprioception but show up as transient spikes in mechanical energy. This paper detects transitions using anomaly detection on energy signals, feeding them to the variational trajectory planner.
CC-STAR: Contact State Transition Estima.how:
The mechanism: Compute instantaneous mechanical power during insertion: P = τ·ω + F·v. During steady contact (peg sliding in hole), power is smooth. Contact transitions (impact with chamfer, binding) cause sharp energy spikes. Train an autoencoder to model steady-state power; when actual power deviates from the reconstruction, a transition is detected.

The planner uses detected transitions to update the contact mode. When a transition occurs, the trajectory online-replans assuming the new contact configuration. This feedback loop enables the variational planner to adapt to contact state changes, improving peg success rate.

Decentralized Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Ag.narr: When agents predict each other's future positions, those predictions have uncertainty. Naive planning treats predicted positions as hard obstacles, ignoring prediction error — agents over-commit to conservative paths. This paper makes each agent's MPPI sampler include neighbor uncertainty ellipsoids, so sampling naturally accounts for prediction error.
Decentralized Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Ag.how:
The mechanism: Each agent broadcasts both its predicted trajectory and a time-varying covariance ellipsoid (uncertainty around the prediction). In the collision-cost function, instead of binary collision/no-collision, compute the probability of overlap between the agent's sampled trajectory and the neighbor's uncertainty ellipsoid. Weight each sample by this collision probability.

Agents that are uncertain about neighbors' positions get softer collision penalties, allowing them to take paths closer to the predicted trajectory. The result: less over-conservative avoidance, tighter formation, while remaining safe even when predictions are inaccurate.

Cooperative Distributed Model Predictive.narr: Distributed MPC typically requires solving many iterations over wireless communication to reach consensus. On resource-constrained robots with slow communication, this becomes a bottleneck. This paper implements full distributed MPC on embedded microcontrollers (no wireless), with consensus solved in just 3 iterations on-chip.
Cooperative Distributed Model Predictive.how:
The mechanism: Each hovercraft has a local embedded processor that runs its own MPC (small state dimension) with a copy of its neighbors' predicted trajectories stored locally. Consensus is achieved via fast parameter-update message passing entirely on-chip. The message passing overhead is milliseconds.

All coordination happens through broadcast of trajectory predictions, with consensus solved immediately (no wait for wireless). This enables kHz-rate formation control on simple embedded CPUs, whereas wireless-based consensus would introduce 10–100 ms latency.

Constrained Learning for Decentralized M.narr: Coverage objectives (each agent covers a region) naturally decompose across agents, but coupling constraints (regions cannot overlap) make the problem non-separable. Naive decentralized learning (each agent learns independently) violates constraints. This paper learns policies subject to explicit constraint satisfaction in the decentralized setting.
Constrained Learning for Decentralized M.how:
The mechanism: Each agent learns a local policy that minimizes coverage error while respecting learned estimates of constraint gradients. Use a dual-variable consensus algorithm: agents broadcast estimates of the Lagrange multipliers for the coupling constraints; each agent's policy is updated using its local constraint gradients and the consensus dual estimate.

Convergence is achieved when each agent's policy satisfies its local constraints and dual estimates converge. The decentralization is key: no agent needs a global view, only broadcasts to neighbors. Coverage constraints are satisfied even though each agent optimizes locally.

POINTWORLD: Scaling 3D World Models for.narr: Physics simulators model rigid body dynamics well but fail on cloth, soft objects, and unknown materials. Learned world models from data generalize better, but training them requires matching state representations. This paper uses point clouds as the state and predicts per-point velocity flow, enabling zero-shot transfer from simulation to real robots.
POINTWORLD: Scaling 3D World Models for.how:
The mechanism: State is a 3D point cloud observed from the camera. The model inputs (cloud + 6-DOF action) and outputs per-point 3D velocities (optical flow). Training uses 50k simulated trajectories. The model is agnostic to object geometry — it learns that certain actions cause predictable point motion regardless of object shape.

At test time on real robots, the point cloud representation automatically handles unseen objects (no geometry preprocessing needed). Planning samples 512 action sequences of length 8; scores each via the learned model (1.8 s for 512×8 rollouts on GPU). Success rate jumps from 18% (simulator-only) to 61% (sim-to-real with learned world model).

Motus: A Unified Latent Action World Mod.narr: Learned world models typically condition on joint commands or action vectors specific to each robot. This breaks generalization across different platforms. This paper learns a unified latent action representation: optical flow. Any action that causes the visual scene to flow in a certain way is modeled identically.
Motus: A Unified Latent Action World Mod.how:
The mechanism: The model takes the current image and optical flow estimate (extracted from any control action via visual odometry) and predicts the next image. During training, compute optical flow from consecutive frames as the latent action variable. The model learns to predict future images conditioned on how the scene is moving, not on platform-specific commands.

At test time, the same model works for different robots because optical flow is universal. A quadrotor that moves left produces the same visual flow as a wheeled robot moving left. The model generalizes to new platforms and morphologies because it operates on task-space (visual flow) rather than control-space (joint commands).

RehearseVLA: Simulated Post-Training for.narr: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) need large amounts of real robot data to learn grounded actions. Simulation is cheap but domain gaps are large. This paper uses a physically-consistent learned world model as a simulator to generate synthetic trajectories that preserve physical plausibility for post-training VLAs.
RehearseVLA: Simulated Post-Training for.how:
The mechanism: Train a world model on real data that predicts state dynamics respecting conservation of energy and momentum. Use this model in a closed-loop rollout: predict next state, check physical consistency (energy conservation), apply a VLA policy trained offline, repeat. Generate diverse synthetic trajectories by sampling different VLA behaviors.

Post-train the VLA on these synthetic trajectories. Because the world model enforces physics, the synthetic data avoids learning shortcuts (e.g., the VLA doesn't learn to predict impossible dynamics). Real-world success improves because the VLA has seen many physically-plausible but never-before-seen situations.

DreamSAC: Learning Hamiltonian World Mod.narr: Learned world models trained on in-distribution data often fail when extrapolating to unseen energy levels or force magnitudes. A model trained on light pushes fails on strong pushes because it has not learned the correct scaling law. This paper learns a Hamiltonian world model that conserves energy, making extrapolation to new energy regimes automatic.
DreamSAC: Learning Hamiltonian World Mod.how:
The mechanism: Parameterize the world model as a Hamiltonian neural network: the state derivative is always ∇H (canonical form). This structural constraint ensures energy conservation by construction. Train on data using contrastive learning to discover symmetries (translations, rotations) that preserve the Hamiltonian structure.

A model trained on manipulation at moderate energies generalizes to higher energies because energy conservation is structural, not learned. The scaling laws (forces increase with speed) follow automatically from the Hamiltonian form. Planning horizons can be longer because energy extrapolation is reliable.

Visual-RRT: Finding Paths toward Visual-.narr: Navigating by visual target — reach a goal configuration where the camera sees a specific image — requires gradients from pixels back to joint angles. A differentiable renderer threads this gradient path, computing how the rendered image changes when the robot moves. Visual-RRT combines this gradient signal with random tree expansion to escape the local minima that pure gradient descent would get stuck in.
Visual-RRT: Finding Paths toward Visual-.how:
The mechanism: The method alternates between two operations: (1) RRT tree expansion — sample random frontier configurations and connect them to the tree; (2) Gradient refinement — from each frontier node, take K gradient steps on the visual loss L = ||I(q) − Igoal||². At each gradient step, the Jacobian ∂I/∂q tells how much each pixel would change with each joint angle.

Why this works: RRT alone would need 61 iterations to find a path in image space because gradient-free search cannot distinguish between a configuration that looks similar to the goal and one that is far away. But rendering is highly multimodal: thousands of different joint configurations can produce nearly identical images. Gradient steps from the differentiable renderer provide a local attractor toward the visual target. Together — global search plus local gradient pull — the combined method escapes spurious local minima in just 8 iterations.

D-Prism: Differentiable Primitives for S.narr: Complex dynamic scenes contain multiple objects moving and interacting, yet a single monolithic neural network struggles to untangle which object caused which motion. D-Prism decomposes the scene into differentiable 3D primitives — boxes, cylinders, meshes — each with its own dynamics parameters. Gradients flow through the geometry, so the optimizer can adjust a primitive's shape and inertia to match observed motion.
D-Prism: Differentiable Primitives for S.how:
The mechanism: The scene is represented as a set of Gaussian or mesh primitives, each with position, rotation, scale, and inertia. Forward pass: render the scene, apply dynamics (integrate momentum under forces and collisions), render the next frame. Backward pass: autodiff through the rendering and dynamics to compute ∂loss/∂(shape, inertia, position).

Why this works: A monolithic world model cannot learn which parameters affect which object. By decomposing the scene, each primitive's gradients point in the direction that would make its motion match observations. An object that slides too far has large error; ∂error/∂friction is negative, so the optimizer increases friction. The geometric structure of primitives lets the gradients point precisely, without the model having to learn the concept of a separate object.

PhysHead: Simulation-Ready Gaussian Head.narr: Animating a realistic human head requires modeling deformable skin and muscle dynamics, yet rasterizing differentiable models is expensive. PhysHead represents the head as differentiable Gaussians with physics-based deformation parameters, enabling high-speed rendering with gradient flow for trajectory optimization of facial expressions and head motion.
PhysHead: Simulation-Ready Gaussian Head.how:
The mechanism: The head avatar is a set of 3D Gaussian splatted primitives. Each Gaussian has a position, covariance, and SH color coefficients. Physics parameters — muscle activation, skin elasticity — are differentiable scalars that modulate the Gaussian positions and covariances. Rendering: splat the deformed Gaussians to image space. Backward: gradient of the image loss flows through the splatting operations back to the physics parameters.

Why this works: Traditional geometry-based avatars (meshes + skinning) require expensive mesh deformation and rendering. Gaussian splatting is O(N) in the number of Gaussians, much faster than mesh rasterization. By making the physics parameters (muscle activation, stiffness) differentiable and treating them as inputs to the splatting operation, trajectory optimization can directly minimize facial expression error without unrolling a separate dynamics simulator.

PhysSkin: Real-Time and Generalizable Ph.narr: Skinning — binding surface deformations to skeletal motion — is traditionally hand-crafted per character, and standard neural skinning ignores forces and contact. PhysSkin learns differentiable skinning weights that recover physics-based deformations from real motion capture data without explicit physics simulation, then generalizes those weights to new characters and motions.
PhysSkin: Real-Time and Generalizable Ph.how:
The mechanism: Given skeleton poses and real surface vertex positions from mocap, the network learns skinning weights w(v, bone) that blend skeleton transformations to deform vertices: v′ = Σbone w(v, bone) · Mbone · v. The weights are functions of vertex position and bone influence — effectively learning spatially-varying blend weights. Training uses reconstruction loss: ||rendered(v′) − reference image||².

Why this works: Neural skinning can capture physics-like behavior (e.g., secondary jiggle, muscle bulge) implicitly without ever running a simulator. Because the weights are differentiable in the skeleton pose, gradient-based trajectory optimization can push on the weights to achieve desired deformations. The self-supervised approach — learning from mocap rather than explicit contact forces — sidesteps the hard problem of contact and material parameter identification, instead capturing what actually happened in the real data.

PAMotion: Physics-Aware Motion Generatio.narr: Generative diffusion models produce motion that looks smooth but ignores Newton's laws — limbs float, feet slip through the ground, hands pass through objects. PAMotion embeds physics loss directly into the diffusion denoising step: object acceleration is computed from generated contact forces and fed back as a differentiable signal that guides the generator toward physically plausible configurations.
PAMotion: Physics-Aware Motion Generatio.how:
The mechanism: At each diffusion denoising step, given the current noisy estimate of the motion, compute contact forces between the human and objects in the scene as a differentiable function (e.g., spring-damper). From Fcontact, compute expected object acceleration: aobj = Fcontact / m. Newton loss: Lphys = ||m·aobj − Fcontact||². Add this physics loss to the score function with weight λ=0.3, then denoise.

Why this works: Pure learned generation has no mechanism to prefer momentum-conserving configurations. Adding the physics loss as a soft constraint means the denoiser's gradient points toward states where forces and accelerations are consistent. The generator learns to produce motion where feet stay planted because slipping would create a large physics error. Interpenetrations increase normal forces, pushing surfaces apart. The result is a generator that has internalized basic biomechanics without explicit simulation.

InterPhys: Physics-aware Human Motion Sy.narr: Humans interact with scenes — walking around obstacles, reaching for objects, catching falling items — yet diffusion models trained on isolated motion sequences have no representation of the scene structure. InterPhys embeds Euler-Lagrange dynamics and damped-spring contact into the motion score function, so the generator reasons about forces and accelerations as it denoises.
InterPhys: Physics-aware Human Motion Sy.how:
The mechanism: The dynamics are encoded as a differentiable score: at each denoising step, compute the skeleton's kinetic and potential energy, and the energy stored in contact springs to the scene geometry. Construct a Lagrangian loss that penalizes inconsistent dynamics: L = ∫ (KE + PE − workby contact) dt. The score ∇L points toward configurations where energy is conserved and contact forces point out of the scene.

Why this works: A standard diffusion model has no way to ensure the generated motion respects contact geometry — it learns statistical correlations from training data, not physical constraints. Embedding Lagrangian mechanics means every denoising step explicitly checks whether the motion makes physical sense. A human walking into a wall receives a contact-force penalty; the denoiser moves the hip back. A falling arm gets penalized by the gravity term; the denoiser spreads the fingers to increase damping. Physics becomes a built-in preference of the generator.

PAD-Hand: Physics-Aware Diffusion for Ha.narr: Recovering 3D hand pose from a single monocular image is ill-posed — many hand configurations project to the same pixels. Physics adds an additional constraint: actual human hands obey gravity and contact laws. PAD-Hand uses Euler-Lagrange residuals as virtual observables during diffusion-based hand pose estimation, pulling the solution toward kinematically and dynamically plausible configurations.
PAD-Hand: Physics-Aware Diffusion for Ha.how:
The mechanism: Given an image and a diffusion-generated hand pose q(t), compute the physics residual: r = ∂L/∂q, where L is the Lagrangian (kinetic minus potential energy). If the hand is accelerating upward against gravity, r is large. During denoising, treat r as a virtual sensor measurement and add it to the likelihood: Ltotal = ||rendered(q) − image||² + λ||r||². Backprop through both image and physics terms to refine q.

Why this works: Image alone is ambiguous: many hand poses produce similar pixels, especially from angles where fingers are foreshortened. Physics residuals break ties: a pose where the hand accelerates impossibly upward has high residual, so the diffusion process steers away from it. The dynamics constraints act like an invisible observer that can see forces and accelerations, narrowing the solution space from infinite possibilities to only those consistent with both appearance and physics.

Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics.narr: Neural dynamics models trained on simulation data fail on real robots because of unmodeled contact softness and material properties. Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics co-trains a simulator prediction with rendered contact from real tactile sensor data, aligning the two worlds without requiring explicit parameter identification or calibration.
Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics.how:
The mechanism: The model consists of two branches: (1) a physics simulator (PyBullet or MuJoCo) predicting next state given current state and action, (2) a neural network predicting contact geometry and forces from tactile readings. Training: collect real robot trajectories with tactile data. For each timestep, run the simulator forward. Render the predicted contact (contact normals, forces) and compare to actual tactile readings. Loss = ||rendered contact − real tactile||² + ||simulator state − real state||².

Why this works: Tactile data is a direct measurement of contact forces that traditional simulators struggle to predict. By using real tactile data as a target for rendering, the model learns to simulate contact as it actually occurs, without ever explicitly identifying material parameters like friction or elasticity. The simulator stays grounded in reality through the tactile loss, while the neural contact model acts as the bridge between simulation and the real world's complexities.

UniPixie: Unified and Probabilistic 3D P.narr: Predicting how sand or clay moves under manipulation requires knowing material parameters — friction angle, cohesion, density — that vary between samples and are usually unknown at prediction time. A single point prediction collapses this uncertainty into overconfidence. UniPixie uses flow matching over material parameter distributions, drawing multiple plausible simulations and aggregating them into a credible interval of outcomes.
UniPixie: Unified and Probabilistic 3D P.how:
The mechanism: Model material parameters θ as a distribution p(θ). Flow matching learns a path from noise to samples of θ: ∇tθ = vθ(θ, t). At inference time, sample K=64 parameter sets from the flow. For each parameter set, run a material-point-method or rigid-body simulator to predict object motion. Aggregate: compute the weighted mean and variance of predicted trajectories.

Why this works: Traditional simulators give one answer: 'the sand pile will settle at angle θ_nominal'. But real sand varies; some is cohesive, some is dry. UniPixie's ensemble covers the range: 92% of real outcomes fall within the model's 90% credible interval. A single-point model (baseline) achieves only 61% coverage because it cannot hedge uncertainty — it commits to one set of parameters. The flow-matching formulation lets the model represent epistemic uncertainty (not knowing the parameters) as an explicit distribution over outcomes, which is the right answer when planning with unknown materials.

NS-Diff: Fluid Navier-Stokes Guided Vide.narr: Generating realistic fluid motion in video requires understanding incompressibility, vorticity, and viscosity — the deep structure of fluid mechanics. NS-Diff guides a video diffusion model with the Navier-Stokes equations and fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning to match real fluid recordings, bridging the physics simulator and the learned generator.
NS-Diff: Fluid Navier-Stokes Guided Vide.how:
The mechanism: The diffusion model's score function is augmented with a Navier-Stokes solver: at each denoising step, evaluate the divergence ∇·v and vorticity ω of the predicted velocity field. Penalize deviations: LNS = ||∇·v||² + λ||∇²v − ∇p||² (viscous term). The gradient ∇LNS flows through the denoiser. Then, RL fine-tuning: use the predicted video as a policy and optimize reward = perceptual similarity to real fluid videos. Critic trained on real fluid data.

Why this works: Unconstrained diffusion generates pixels that look fluid-like but violate momentum conservation — water appears to teleport or leave gaps. The Navier-Stokes guidance acts like a physics checker that continuously asks: 'does this velocity field satisfy the equations of motion?' If not, the penalty pushes the denoiser toward physically consistent flow. RL fine-tuning then aligns the guided generator with real-world recordings, where unmodeled turbulence and boundary conditions are present. The result: generated fluid that both obeys the equations and matches reality.

Goal Force: Teaching Video Models To Acc.narr: Video generation models produce visually smooth sequences but are often agnostic to the physical outcome — a generated hand might push an object without exerting enough force for it to move. Goal Force conditions the generator on a 3-channel ControlNet tensor encoding force magnitude, goal position, and object mass, teaching the model to generate motion that will reliably accomplish the task.
Goal Force: Teaching Video Models To Acc.how:
The mechanism: A ControlNet encoder maps (force, goal location, mass) to a 3-channel spatial feature map, one channel per condition type. This is concatenated with the noisy video frames before the UNet denoiser. During training, supervision comes from paired data: real manipulation videos labeled with estimated forces (from IMU or visual tracking) and outcomes (did the object reach the goal?). Loss = ||generated frames − real frames||² + λ·||object final position − goal||².

Why this works: An unconditioned generator averages over all training data; it produces safe, realistic-looking motion that may be too gentle to move heavy objects. By conditioning on explicit force and goal information, the generator learns to scale motion intensity to the task. High-force requests produce faster, more vigorous motions; heavy-object requests produce different contact patterns. The result: 75–100% success rate on visual planning tasks, compared to much lower rates for unconditional baselines.

InterPrior: Scaling Generative Control f.narr: Learning to generate realistic human-object interactions from demonstrations is sample-efficient with imitation but brittle; pure RL is stable but sample-hungry. InterPrior trains an imitation expert (VAE) on expert demonstrations, then scales it with RL fine-tuning, combining the data efficiency of supervised learning with the task-performance of reinforcement learning.
InterPrior: Scaling Generative Control f.how:
The mechanism: Stage 1: train a goal-conditioned VAE on expert interaction sequences. Encoder: motion (pose, hand position) → latent z. Decoder: (z, goal state) → predicted next motion. Loss = reconstruction + KL. Stage 2: Use the VAE as a policy: sample z ∼ p(z), decode (z, goal) → asuggested. Run on simulated human and objects. Reward: progress toward goal + physical plausibility (no interpenetration, reasonable contact forces). RL (PPO) optimizes log p(z) and the goal embedding.

Why this works: Imitation learning alone gives smooth, natural-looking motion but may not push hard enough or take risky shortcuts to achieve the goal. RL alone needs thousands of samples to learn what interactions work. The two-stage approach: the VAE prior keeps the policy close to expert behavior (high probability z values correspond to realistic motion), while RL tunes it to actually accomplish the task. Stage 1 provides a strong prior; Stage 2 refines it. The result is a policy that is both sample-efficient and capable of generalizing to unseen interaction types beyond the training data.
